\caption{\textbf{What a deployment gets at each rate it might have shipped, and never tunes.} Every entry is mean adaptation benefit \% / how many of the 216 cells ended up \emph{worse} than the frozen model. A \colorbox[gray]{0.88}{shaded} cell marked $\bullet$ is one a deployment could ship: it leaves no cell below the frozen model, \emph{and} what it gives up against the best tuned rule is under 2 points with 95\% confidence. \textbf{The band is the longest unbroken run of shaded cells in a row}, i.e.\ the whole range of rates that could have been chosen before seeing the site without regret. It is given twice: as a count of rates, which the reader can check against the row, and as its width in decades, which is what a deployment experiences. The two are not interchangeable -- the rates here are 0.5 decades apart, so a run of $n$ of them spans $0.5(n{-}1)$ decades and a single rate spans none. A wide band means nobody has to pick the rate; a one-cell band means the rule works at exactly the rate it happens to ship with. Two notes on the criterion: the comparison against the tuned rule is \emph{paired} per cell, because every rule is read on the same cells and the uncertainty in a difference is far smaller than in either mean; and harmlessness alone is passed by 7 of the rules listed here, plain SGD among them, which is why being competitive is part of the criterion at all. Only class representatives are listed; every other rule in Table~\ref{tab:optimizers} has a band of one rate or none. $\ddagger$ RelSign has no learning rate -- its lr \emph{is} $\tau$ -- so its row reads sensitivity to its own constant, which is what the ablation asks.}
